\end{proof}

The carrier never changes: only the family of subsets designated open changes. ``Collapse'' therefore means loss of observable status, not deletion of points.

\section{Finite algorithms}

\begin{algorithm}[Consensus intersection]
Given a finite carrier $X$ and channel topologies $\mathcal T_1,\ldots,\mathcal T_n$, each represented as a hash set of immutable subsets, initialize $\mathcal C=\mathcal T_1$ and successively replace $\mathcal C$ by $\mathcal C\cap\mathcal T_i$. Return $\mathcal C$.
\end{algorithm}

If every topology has at most $M$ open sets, expected running time is $O(nM)$ membership operations, excluding subset encoding. Since a topology on a $q$-point set can have $2^q$ opens, explicit representation is exponential in $q$ in the worst case.

\begin{algorithm}[Strict-collapse witness search]
Given an old consensus $\mathcal C$ and new topology $\mathcal S$, scan $A\in\mathcal C$. Return the first $A\notin\mathcal S$; if none exists, report that consensus is unchanged.
\end{algorithm}

With hash membership, this takes expected time $O(|\mathcal C|)$. Its correctness is the strictness criterion.

A grid demonstration on the real line can display directional interval predicates and show that $[0,1)$ is accepted by the lower-facing rule but fails a symmetric neighborhood test at $0$. Such a grid is illustrative rather than a proof of the infinite-space identity, because clipping and endpoint effects can alter topology. Exact finite experiments should specify genuine finite topologies and intersect their open-set families.

\section{Applications}

\subsection{Conservative multisensor fusion}
If a controller acts only on regions certified by every sensor, its operational event structure is a consensus topology. A new sensor cannot create unanimously certified events. A lost open set is an explicit disagreement witness, making strict changes auditable.

\subsection{Neural-state readouts}
For a finite neural transition graph, one may assign each readout the topology generated by subsets it can reliably distinguish. Consensus then records distinctions stable across every readout. This requires empirical definitions of distinguishability, noise tolerance, and fusion policy. Once supplied, the strictness criterion is testable by finite enumeration.

\subsection{Scientific observability}
Different experimental modalities may support different robust event families. Their consensus captures conditions invariant across protocols, rather than the union of everything detected somewhere. A union of topologies need not itself be a topology, while their intersection always is.

\subsection{Continuity}
Changing consensus changes continuity. Coarsening the topology on a codomain generally makes continuity into it easier; coarsening the topology on a domain generally makes continuity out of it harder. Observer architecture can therefore affect which transformations count as observationally smooth.

\section{Limitations}
The unanimity rule is a modeling choice. Majority, weighted, and confidence-threshold fusion need not produce a topology without an additional closure operation. Channel count is also a coarse complexity measure: duplicate channels change nothing, while one channel may resolve many more opens than several others.

Topology omits metric, probabilistic, and temporal information. It records qualitative stability, not distance, likelihood, latency, or noise. The real-line channels are ideal directional resolutions, whereas physical sensors have finite precision. Empirical use may require finite generated topologies, measures, filtrations, or probabilistic neighborhoods.

Most importantly, the theorem does not imply that physical spacetime changes when observed. It says that a topology defined as unanimous observability depends on the chosen channel family. An ontological claim requires premises not contained in this model.

\section{Future work}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em]
\item \textbf{Finite observer-complexity monotonicity.} Develop a uniform indexed theorem for extensions from $n$ to $n+1$ channels.
\item \textbf{Strictness under extension.} Extract computable witnesses for consensus loss on finite spaces.
\item \textbf{Minimal observer complexity.} For a finite $X$ and target topology $\mathcal T$, find the least $n$ for which $\mathcal T$ is the consensus of $n$ strict refinements, and bound it using $|\mathcal T|$.
\item \textbf{Product compositionality.} Characterize when consensus of channelwise products equals the product of the two consensus topologies.
\item \textbf{Empirical encoding.} Generate readout topologies from measured distinguishability data and test channel-addition predictions.
\item \textbf{Approximate consensus.} Study threshold agreement, whose accepted family need not itself be topological.
\item \textbf{Dynamic channels.} Analyze abrupt changes in consensus as channel topologies vary over time.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Discussion}
Euclidean geometry emerges here as common ground between two directionally biased resolutions. This is not metric averaging or probabilistic mixing; it is logical conjunction of openness. All Euclidean opens survive both channels. A set with only a right-facing certificate can fail the upper-limit test, and vice versa. What survives both has two one-sided certificates at every point, which combine into an ordinary interval.

The witness $[0,1)$ localizes the phenomenon at its left endpoint. Lower-limit geometry permits a neighborhood beginning exactly at $0$ and extending rightward. Euclidean geometry demands room on both sides. The added upper-limit channel imposes that missing demand, removing the half-open region from common certification.

Consensus is thus antitone in constraints: adding tests may increase private evidence while shrinking the feasible family that passes every test. Topology makes this familiar logical fact geometrically consequential.

\section{Conclusion}
A finite network of topological channels has a natural conservative observable geometry: the intersection of its channel topologies. Adding one channel intersects the old consensus with one more topology, so it can only preserve or remove open regions. Strict change occurs exactly when the new channel vetoes an old consensus-open set.

On $\R$, one lower-limit channel observes lower-limit geometry, whereas adding its upper-limit counterpart yields precisely Euclidean geometry. The inclusion is strict, witnessed by $[0,1)$. The same carrier therefore supports networks of complexities one and two with different observable geometries. The model does not turn observation into metaphysics; it turns agreement into topology, providing a precise mechanism suitable for finite computation and, given an empirical encoding, falsifiable application.

"""Numerical illustrations of consensus topology and one-sided collapse.

The finite example computes exact intersections of explicitly listed topologies.

lower-limit open but not Euclidean open. No third-party packages are required.

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import FrozenSet, Iterable, Sequence, TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")
FiniteSet = FrozenSet[T]
Topology = FrozenSet[FiniteSet[T]]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ProbeResult:
    """Result of testing a neighborhood around one sampled point."""

    point: float
    lower_neighborhood: tuple[float, float]
    lower_fits: bool
    symmetric_neighborhood: tuple[float, float]
    symmetric_fits: bool


def powerset(items: Sequence[T]) -> list[FiniteSet[T]]:
    """Return every subset of a short finite sequence as a frozenset."""
    result: list[FiniteSet[T]] = []
    for mask in range(1 << len(items)):
        result.append(
            frozenset(items[index] for index in range(len(items)) if mask & (1 << index))
        )
    return result


def is_topology(carrier: FiniteSet[T], family: Topology[T]) -> bool:
    """Check the topology axioms by exhaustive finite enumeration."""
    empty: FiniteSet[T] = frozenset()
    if empty not in family or carrier not in family:
        return False
    # On a finite family, closure under binary unions implies arbitrary-union closure.
    for left in family:
        for right in family:
            if (left | right) not in family or (left & right) not in family:
                return False
    return True


def consensus(topologies: Sequence[Topology[T]]) -> Topology[T]:
    """Intersect the open-set families of all channels."""
    if not topologies:
        raise ValueError("At least one channel is required")
    shared = set(topologies[0])
    for topology in topologies[1:]:
        shared.intersection_update(topology)
    return frozenset(shared)


def collapse_witness(old_consensus: Topology[T], new_channel: Topology[T]) -> FiniteSet[T] | None:
    """Find an old consensus-open set vetoed by a new channel, if one exists."""
    rejected = old_consensus.difference(new_channel)
    if not rejected:
        return None
    return min(rejected, key=lambda subset: (len(subset), tuple(sorted(map(str, subset)))))


def in_half_open_unit_interval(x: float) -> bool:
    """Membership predicate for [0, 1)."""
    return 0.0 <= x < 1.0


def probe_half_open_interval(points: Iterable[float], radius: float = 0.1) -> list[ProbeResult]:
    """Sample directional and symmetric neighborhoods inside [0, 1).

    For each point x, the lower-limit test uses [x, x + delta), while the
    Euclidean test uses (x - delta, x + delta). Endpoint containment is tested
    numerically using representative points just inside each neighborhood.
    """
    if radius <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("radius must be positive")
    results: list[ProbeResult] = []
    for x in points:
        delta = min(radius, max((1.0 - x) / 2.0, radius / 1000.0))
        lower = (x, x + delta)
        symmetric = (x - delta, x + delta)
        lower_samples = (x, x + delta / 2.0, x + 0.999 * delta)
        symmetric_samples = (x - 0.999 * delta, x, x + 0.999 * delta)
        results.append(
            ProbeResult(
                point=x,
                lower_neighborhood=lower,
                lower_fits=all(in_half_open_unit_interval(y) for y in lower_samples),
                symmetric_neighborhood=symmetric,
                symmetric_fits=all(in_half_open_unit_interval(y) for y in symmetric_samples),

        )
    return results

    print(f"  two-channel open sets: {len(two_channel)}")
    print("  consensus after adding the opposite channel:")

    print()

    run_finite_example()
    run_real_line_probe()

    (survivingCandidates candidates checks).card ≤ candidates.card := by
  exact Finset.card_le_card (survivingCandidates_subset candidates checks)

/-- If one ambient candidate fails a check, filtering gives a strict reduction
in search-space cardinality. -/
theorem survivingCandidates_card_lt {α : Type*} [DecidableEq α]
    (candidates : Finset α) (checks : List (α → Prop)) (a : α)
    (ha : a ∈ candidates) (hfail : ¬ Passes checks a) :
    (survivingCandidates candidates checks).card < candidates.card := by
  classical
  apply Finset.card_lt_card
  rw [Finset.ssubset_iff_subset_ne]
  refine ⟨survivingCandidates_subset candidates checks, ?_⟩
  intro heq
  have ha' : a ∈ survivingCandidates candidates checks := by
    rw [heq]
    exact ha
  exact hfail (Finset.mem_filter.mp (by simpa [survivingCandidates] using ha')).2

/-- If the verified checks isolate a unique target, their propositions form a
backward certificate for candidate equality. -/
theorem unique_survivor_gives_backward_certificate
    {α : Type*} (checks : List (α → Prop)) (a target : α)
    (hunique : Passes checks a → a = target) :
    BackwardCertificate (a = target) (checks.map fun check => check a) := by
  intro hall
  apply hunique
  intro check hcheck
  apply hall (check a)
  exact List.mem_map.mpr ⟨check, hcheck, rfl⟩

/-- Search completeness: a target in the ambient candidate set that passes all
checks remains in the filtered set. -/
theorem target_mem_survivingCandidates {α : Type*} [DecidableEq α]
    (candidates : Finset α) (checks : List (α → Prop)) (target : α)
    (hmem : target ∈ candidates) (hpasses : Passes checks target) :
    target ∈ survivingCandidates candidates checks := by
  classical
  simp [survivingCandidates, hmem, hpasses]

/-- Three elementary arithmetic consequences used to identify `6` among the
natural numbers below `8`.  They are formulas of first-order arithmetic and so
provide a small Peano-arithmetic calibration of consequence-guided filtering. -/
def sixChecks : List (ℕ → Prop) :=
  [fun n => 0 < n, fun n => 2 ∣ n, fun n => 3 ∣ n]

/-- The three arithmetic checks isolate exactly `6` in the finite search space

theorem sixChecks_unique :
    survivingCandidates (Finset.range 8) sixChecks = {6} := by
  classical
  ext n
  simp [survivingCandidates, Passes, sixChecks]
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨hn8, hn0, ⟨k, hk⟩, ⟨j, hj⟩⟩
    omega
  · intro hn
    omega

one; the surviving-cardinality ratio is therefore exactly `1/8`. -/
theorem sixChecks_compression_measure :
    (survivingCandidates (Finset.range 8) sixChecks).card = 1 ∧
      (Finset.range 8).card = 8 := by
  rw [sixChecks_unique]
  simp

    BackwardCertificate (n = 6) (sixChecks.map fun check => check n) := by
  apply unique_survivor_gives_backward_certificate sixChecks n 6

    apply target_mem_survivingCandidates
    · simpa using hn
    · exact hx

Conjecture: there is no universal constant `c < 1` such that every consequence-stable proposition has total certified cost at most `c` times its shortest direct proof. A counterexample family would consist of propositions whose shortest backward certificates asymptotically reproduce their shortest direct proofs.

not depend on the alphabet being Boolean. A local rule that reads one site and
then applies an alphabet permutation is reversible over every alphabet.

/-- Configurations over an arbitrary alphabet. -/

/-- Radius-one local rules over an arbitrary alphabet. -/
abbrev LocalRuleOver (α : Type*) := α → α → α → α

/-- The cyclic global map of an arbitrary-alphabet radius-one rule. -/
def globalMapOver {α : Type*} (f : LocalRuleOver α) {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n)
    (x : ConfigOver α n) : ConfigOver α n :=
  fun i => f (x (leftIdx hn i)) (x i) (x (rightIdx hn i))

/-- Applying an alphabet equivalence after permuting the sites is an equivalence
of configuration spaces. -/
def coordinateAlphabetEquiv {α : Type*} {n : ℕ}
    (p : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) (e : Equiv.Perm α) :
    ConfigOver α n ≃ ConfigOver α n where
  toFun x i := e (x (p i))
  invFun x i := e.symm (x (p.symm i))
  left_inv x := by
    funext i
    simp
  right_inv x := by
    funext i
    simp

/-- Configuration equivalences compose by independent composition of site and
alphabet permutations. -/
theorem coordinateAlphabetEquiv_trans {α : Type*} {n : ℕ}
    (p q : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) (e d : Equiv.Perm α) :
    (coordinateAlphabetEquiv p e).trans (coordinateAlphabetEquiv q d) =
      coordinateAlphabetEquiv (p * q) (d * e) := by
  ext x i
  change d (e (x (p (q i)))) = d (e (x (p (q i))))
  rfl

/-- A radius-one rule obtained by applying an alphabet permutation to any one
of its three inputs has bijective dynamics on every nonempty finite cycle. -/
theorem single_coordinate_rule_bijective {α : Type*} {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n)
    (f : LocalRuleOver α) (e : Equiv.Perm α)
    (hf : (∀ l c r, f l c r = e l) ∨
      (∀ l c r, f l c r = e c) ∨
      (∀ l c r, f l c r = e r)) :
    Function.Bijective (globalMapOver f hn) := by
  rw [Function.bijective_iff_has_inverse]
  rcases hf with hl | hc | hr
  · refine ⟨(fun x i => e.symm (x (rightIdx hn i))), ?_, ?_⟩
    · intro x
      funext i
      simp only [globalMapOver, hl, Equiv.symm_apply_apply, leftIdx_rightIdx]
    · intro x
      funext i
      simp only [globalMapOver, hl, rightIdx_leftIdx, Equiv.apply_symm_apply]
  · refine ⟨(fun x i => e.symm (x i)), ?_, ?_⟩
    · intro x
      funext i
      simp only [globalMapOver, hc, Equiv.symm_apply_apply]
    · intro x
      funext i
      simp only [globalMapOver, hc, Equiv.apply_symm_apply]
  · refine ⟨(fun x i => e.symm (x (leftIdx hn i))), ?_, ?_⟩
    · intro x
      funext i
      simp only [globalMapOver, hr, Equiv.symm_apply_apply, rightIdx_leftIdx]
    · intro x
      funext i
      simp only [globalMapOver, hr, leftIdx_rightIdx, Equiv.apply_symm_apply]

/-- The inverse dynamics of a left-reading permutative rule is the right shift
followed by the inverse alphabet permutation. -/
theorem left_rule_explicit_inverse {α : Type*} {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n)
    (f : LocalRuleOver α) (e : Equiv.Perm α)
    (hf : ∀ l c r, f l c r = e l) :
    Function.LeftInverse
      (fun x i => e.symm (x (rightIdx hn i)))
      (globalMapOver f hn) ∧
    Function.RightInverse
      (fun x i => e.symm (x (rightIdx hn i)))
      (globalMapOver f hn) := by
  constructor <;> intro x <;> funext i
  · simp only [globalMapOver, hf, Equiv.symm_apply_apply, leftIdx_rightIdx]
  · simp only [globalMapOver, hf, rightIdx_leftIdx, Equiv.apply_symm_apply]
